paras: The Rome sidewalk clash was a street confrontation on the afternoon of August 23, 1890, in Rome, Georgia, in which two white men struck and knocked down a Black man after a sidewalk collision while a white crowd urged them on. Other Black men joined the fight, police made one or two arrests, and a Rome dispatch described it as a near "serious conflict between whites and blacks."

According to the dispatch, Capt. Ramey, "a rather elderly gentleman," was walking in front of Vandiver's saloon in the lower part of the city when a Black man pushing a baby carriage ran against him and pushed him off the sidewalk. When Ramey asked what he meant, the man was said to have cursed him, and Ramey hit him with his umbrella. The man then attacked Ramey, but Conductor Hal Hawkins, who was standing nearby, knocked him down.
A large crowd gathered, with whites yelling "let him maul the stuffing out of him." Other Black men joined in, and for a time a general fight seemed likely.

Policemen arrived and made "one or two arrests," and order took about half an hour to restore. Among those arrested was Tom Sparks, a Black man held for drawing a pistol, whom the paper called "a desperate negro" and said had shot a man at Birmingham a few days before. No report of charges against Ramey or Hawkins, or of any court hearing, appears in the coverage.

The only account found ran on the front page of the Savannah Morning News on August 24 under the headlines "A CLASH OF COLORS" and "Whites and Blacks Ready for a Fracas at Rome." The dispatch told the story from the white side, placing the start of the trouble on the Black man's collision and cursing and naming none of the Black participants except Sparks, whom it cast as dangerous. No Black-press report of the incident was found.

accounts.label: Rome dispatch
accounts.gist: The Black man ran into Ramey with a baby carriage and cursed him; Ramey struck him with an umbrella, the man attacked Ramey, and Hawkins knocked him down, after which a crowd gathered and police restored order.

framing.detail: Called it 'A CLASH OF COLORS' and a near 'serious conflict between whites and blacks', blamed the Black man for the collision and cursing, and labeled the arrested Sparks 'a desperate negro'; it also printed the white crowd's cry to 'maul the stuffing out of him'.
